questions.q: A writer wants three characters to carry a history of a mass movement. What did Wilkerson do in The Warmth of Other Suns?
choices: Chose three people who met in the same city
Chose one person from each main stream of the migration, from more than 1,200 interviews, so together they cover the whole
Invented three composite characters
Picked the three most famous migrants
questions.explain: Each strand covers ground the others can't: different routes, decades and lives.

questions.q: Burnham and Holmes never meet in The Devil in the White City. How does the braid still work?
choices: By contrast: alternating light and dark, the fair and the murders color each other
It doesn't; readers wait for a meeting that never comes
Through a framing narrator who links them
By convergence in the final chapter
questions.explain: A contrast braid gets its meaning from comparison, not collision.

questions.q: Where should a writer usually switch from one strand to another?
choices: At a resting point, when a strand's episode is complete
At chapter lengths fixed in advance
At a moment of tension, so the reader is pulled through the next strand to get back
Only at the midpoint
questions.explain: Cutting on tension is the slowed-down version of cross-cutting in a chase.

questions.q: How is Killers of the Flower Moon structured?
choices: Strict alternation between Mollie Burkhart and Tom White
A five-act pyramid
In reverse chronological order
Three chronicles in sequence: the victim's family, the investigator, then Grann's own reporting, which questions the tidy ending
questions.explain: It's a braid laid end to end, each chronicle re-seeing what came before.

questions.q: A heist film follows a safecracker, a driver and an inside man, all heading toward the night of the job. What kind of braid is this?
choices: A contrast braid
A convergence braid
A frame story
A picaresque
questions.explain: The strands head toward a meeting the audience is waiting for.

questions.q: In Stoppard's Arcadia, scenes from 1809 and the present alternate in the same room, and in the last scene both share the stage. What does that show about braiding on stage?
choices: Theatre can't braid without film techniques
The two periods must be played by the same actors
A single space can hold strands from different times, letting them meet without the characters meeting
It's an example of the unity of time
questions.explain: Theatre braids by sharing one set across periods, converging in the final image.

questions.q: Your draft braids four strands, and two of them show nearly the same thing. What's the braid-maker's advice?
choices: Cut or merge one: every strand should cover ground the others can't
Alternate them more strictly
Add a fifth strand to balance them
Move them both to the end
questions.explain: Strands are chosen, not found; redundancy dilutes the braid.

ideas: Choose each strand so it shows something the others can't, and cut any that duplicates another.
Let two lives that never meet sit side by side, so the comparison makes the meaning.
Tell the same events in three successive parts from different viewpoints, ending with the writer's own investigation overturning the tidy solution.
Switch between storylines at a moment of tension, so the reader hurries through one to get back to the other.
